promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Observations and case studies in qualitative research
Generalization and ethics in qualitative research

questions.q: A focus group is a form of interview in which:
options: A small group discusses a topic together, guided by a moderator
One participant answers a fixed questionnaire
Behaviour is observed without any questions
questions.explain: Focus groups collect data from group interaction and discussion, which can generate rich, spontaneous responses.

questions.q: An unstructured interview differs from a structured interview because it:
options: Has no fixed set of questions and develops conversationally
questions.explain: Unstructured interviews follow the participant's lead with few preset questions, maximising depth but reducing comparability.

questions.q: A semi-structured interview typically uses:
options: A guide of core questions plus freedom to probe further
A rigid script with no deviation
questions.explain: Semi-structured interviews balance consistency across participants with the flexibility to explore individual responses.

questions.q: A researcher wants to explore, flexibly and in depth, how individuals cope with grief. The most suitable method is:
questions.explain: Sensitive, experiential topics are best explored through flexible qualitative interviewing that allows follow-up.

questions.q: A limitation of interview methods is that responses may be affected by:
questions.explain: Participants may present themselves favourably or be influenced by the interviewer, biasing the data.

questions.q: In participant observation, the researcher:
options: Takes part in the group or setting being studied
questions.explain: Participant observation involves the researcher joining the group, which can give insider insight but risks losing objectivity.

questions.q: A strength of covert observation is reduced participant reactivity, but its main drawback is:
options: Ethical concerns about the lack of informed consent
That it must use numerical scales
That it always occurs in a laboratory
questions.explain: Because participants do not know they are observed, covert observation behaves more naturally but raises consent and privacy issues.

questions.q: A naturalistic observation is carried out:
questions.explain: Naturalistic observation studies behaviour in real settings, giving high ecological validity.

questions.q: A researcher joins a subculture without revealing their identity to study its practices from the inside. This is:
options: Covert participant observation, which raises ethical issues
questions.explain: Joining the group secretly is covert participant observation; the lack of consent creates significant ethical concerns.

questions.q: In qualitative research, a case study typically:
options: Uses multiple methods to build an in-depth understanding of one case
Relies on a single reaction-time measure
questions.explain: Case studies triangulate methods (interviews, observation, documents) to understand a case holistically.

questions.q: Purposive sampling in qualitative research selects participants who:
options: Possess characteristics or experiences relevant to the research question
questions.explain: Purposive sampling deliberately targets information-rich cases suited to the study's aims.

questions.q: Snowball sampling works by:
options: Having existing participants recruit others they know
Selecting every tenth person on a list
Assigning participants with a random number generator
questions.explain: Snowball sampling is useful for reaching hidden or hard-to-access populations through participants' networks.

questions.q: Theoretical sampling involves continuing to collect data until:
options: No new themes or insights emerge (saturation)
A significance level of 0.05 is reached
questions.explain: Sampling continues until theoretical saturation, when additional data no longer add new categories or insights.

questions.q: To study members of a hidden, hard-to-reach community, a researcher asks each participant to introduce others. This is:
questions.explain: Recruiting through participants' referrals (snowball sampling) is well suited to hard-to-reach populations.

questions.q: In qualitative research, 'credibility' is broadly the counterpart to which criterion in quantitative research?
questions.explain: Within trustworthiness criteria, credibility parallels internal validity: whether findings genuinely reflect participants' realities.

questions.q: Reflexivity in qualitative research means that the researcher:
options: Critically reflects on how their own role and assumptions shape the research
Repeats the study exactly to check reliability
questions.explain: Reflexivity involves acknowledging and examining the researcher's influence on data collection and interpretation.

questions.q: Common forms of triangulation include method, data, theory and:
questions.explain: Using multiple researchers, methods, data sources or theories to cross-check findings strengthens credibility.

questions.q: Researcher bias occurs when:
options: The researcher's expectations influence how data are gathered or interpreted
questions.explain: Preconceptions can shape questioning, coding and interpretation; reflexivity and triangulation help limit this bias.

questions.q: A researcher keeps a reflexive journal throughout a study. The main purpose is to:
options: Monitor how their own assumptions may be affecting the research
questions.explain: A reflexive journal documents the researcher's evolving perspective, supporting transparency and credibility.

questions.q: In qualitative research, transferability refers to:
options: The extent to which findings might apply to other contexts, judged with rich description
The exact replication of numerical results
The manipulation of an independent variable
questions.explain: Rather than statistical generalization, qualitative research offers thick description so readers can judge transferability to their own contexts.

questions.q: Types of generalization discussed in qualitative research include representational, inferential and:
questions.explain: Qualitative work may generalise to theory (theoretical generalization) rather than to populations via statistics.

questions.q: Informed consent is especially important in qualitative interviews because participants often:
options: Share personal and potentially sensitive information
Do not interact with the researcher
questions.explain: The depth and sensitivity of qualitative data make genuine informed consent and careful handling essential.

questions.q: A participant discloses sensitive personal details in an interview. To act ethically, the researcher should:
options: Anonymise the data and keep it confidential
questions.explain: Protecting identity through anonymisation and confidentiality safeguards participants who share sensitive information.

questions.q: Qualitative findings are usually not generalized in the same way as quantitative results because:
options: Samples are small and purposive rather than large and random
questions.explain: Small, purposive samples support depth and theoretical or transferable insight rather than statistical generalization to populations.
